in foods (e.g., milk and heat-processed cereal grains). Human proteins consist of only L-AAs and glycine, but certain bacterial
peptides contain D-AAs (e.g., D-proline, D-alanine, and D-glutamate). Some non-proteinogenic AAs [e.g., GABA, b-alanine, and
taurine (which have important physiological roles in humans), and aminomalonic acid (which is present as a free AA in humans
and microbes)] have no D- or L-isomers. The chemical conﬁguration of AAs is not changed in their crystalline form. All L-AAs plus
glycine are the most abundant physiological isomers and account for > 99.9% of total AAs in humans.
The nomenclature of an AA with more than one asymmetric carbon includes an allo-form. For example, a synthetic L-threonine
(a 4-carbon AA) whose b-carbon has a conﬁguration opposite to that of the a-carbon is called L-allo-threonine. L-Threonine and
L-allo-threonine are called diastereomers, and the relationship between the two AAs is diastereomerism. Likewise, a synthetic
L-isoleucine (a 5-carbon AA) whose b-carbon has a conﬁguration opposite to that of the a-carbon has a diastereomer of L-allo-
isoleucine. This also applies to synthetic D-threonine and D-isoleucine.
